title: Colorado window tint laws: what to check before you install
description: A practical Colorado Springs guide to visible light transmission, rear glass, windshield strips and why the vehicle-and-glass combination matters.

sections.title: Start with the actual Colorado rule
sections.text: Colorado Revised Statutes section 42-4-227 is the place to start. In the current official title-42 printout, the windshield must allow at least 70% light transmittance. For a vehicle registered in Colorado, windows other than the windshield generally may not allow less than 27% light transmittance. Those numbers describe the light passing through the installed window combination, not a promise that a film labeled with a number will produce that result on every vehicle. Factory glass, existing film and the new film all affect the reading.

sections.title: Rear glass has a specific exception
sections.text: The statute says windows to the rear of the driver, including the rear window, may allow less than 27% when the windshield and front side windows allow at least 70%. That is why a dark-looking rear window cannot be evaluated by itself. The front side glass and windshield still matter. The law also addresses metallic or mirrored appearance, which is prohibited, and permits a nontransparent strip at the top of the windshield only under stated conditions about height, color, vision and glare.

sections.title: Treat a percentage as a measurement
sections.text: Visible light transmission, or VLT, is a useful specification when comparing film. It is not the same as a legal approval. Ask the installer what the proposed film is, what glass it will be applied over, and how the combined result will be checked. If the vehicle has factory privacy glass, an older film or unusual glass, a shade that looked acceptable on another car may not produce the same measurement here.

sections.title: What to bring to a quote
sections.text: Send the year, make and model, the glass you want treated, and photos of any existing tint. Mention whether you drive at night, cross state lines or need a windshield strip. Auto Vos can discuss a film and coverage plan, but the final compliance question belongs to the current statute and the specific vehicle. Laws and official guidance can change, so confirm the current text before installation.

title: How much does window tint cost in Colorado Springs?
description: Window tint prices depend on your car, the film and which windows you want tinted. Here’s what to include when asking for a quote.

sections.title: Why do window tint prices vary?
sections.text: A tint quote depends on the vehicle and the glass being treated. A compact coupe with two front doors is a different job from an SUV with a large rear hatch, a panoramic roof or several rows of glass. The cleanest way to compare quotes is to ask each shop to name the included windows, film family, shade and preparation. A low number can mean less glass, a different film or no allowance for removing old material.

sections.title: Film choice changes the job
sections.text: Film is more than darkness. XPEL's PRIME specification sheet lists variant-specific visible light transmission, solar-energy, infrared and UV values. That means a darker appearance does not automatically tell you how a film will perform in heat, glare or UV rejection. Ask what the proposed film is designed to do and what the measured specification means on your vehicle. If comfort is the priority, compare the film's performance data and the glass coverage rather than shopping by shade alone.

sections.title: Preparation belongs in the quote
sections.text: Existing tint, adhesive residue, contamination, difficult seals and unusual glass shapes can add labor. A careful shop needs to know whether old film is peeling, bubbling or already on the glass. Ask whether removal, cleaning and curing instructions are included. The final price should also make clear whether a windshield, sunroof, quarter glass or rear hatch is included, because those pieces can change access and installation time.

sections.title: How do I get a window tint quote?
sections.text: Send us your car’s year, make and model and the windows you want tinted. Tell us if you want less heat, less glare or more privacy, and whether old tint needs removing. Photos of the glass help. We’ll discuss the film and shade, price, drop-off time and care instructions before you book.

title: How much does PPF cost in Colorado Springs?
description: Full-front and full-body PPF cover different amounts of your car. The film, panel shapes and paint preparation also affect the price.

sections.title: Is full-body PPF more expensive than full-front PPF?
sections.text: Yes, full-body PPF uses more film and takes more installation time. Full-front coverage focuses on the front of the car; the exact panels included should be listed in your quote. Ask whether the hood and fenders are covered in full or only partway, and where you will see edges or seams.

sections.title: Which film am I paying for?
sections.text: XPEL describes ULTIMATE PLUS as a clear-coated polyurethane film designed to help protect paint from stone chips and abrasion. Its clear coat uses elastomeric polymers that allow light scratches to heal over time. Those are product characteristics, not a guarantee against every chip or impact. Confirm the film family, finish and any written warranty terms in the quote. If satin or another appearance is being considered, view the finish on the vehicle's paint before approving it.

sections.title: Preparation and paint condition matter
sections.text: PPF is installed over a surface that must be clean and suitable. Existing chips, scratches, repainted panels, contamination and older protection can change preparation. Film does not restore missing paint or erase damage underneath. Send photos or arrange an inspection so the shop can say what preparation is included and what condition limits the result.

sections.title: What should my PPF quote include?
sections.text: Your PPF quote should list the film and finish, each covered panel, paint preparation and price. It should also explain visible seams, edge treatment, timing and warranty terms. Send us your car’s year, make and model and the panels you want protected. Include photos of any chips, scratches or old film so we can account for that work.

title: PPF vs. ceramic coating: which does my car need?
description: Choose PPF for help against small chips and scuffs. Choose ceramic coating for easier cleaning. You can use both.

sections.title: PPF is the physical barrier
sections.text: Paint protection film is a film installed over selected painted panels. XPEL describes ULTIMATE PLUS as a clear-coated polyurethane film designed to help protect against stone chips and abrasion, with a topcoat that can heal light scratches. That makes PPF the more relevant conversation when your concern is road debris reaching the paint. It still is not armor: serious impacts, collisions, deep damage and poor care can exceed what the film can handle.

sections.title: What does ceramic coating do?
sections.text: Ceramic coating forms a thin layer over prepared paint or compatible PPF. It helps water and dirt release from the surface, making washing easier. It does not provide the same physical protection as film and will not stop rock chips. You still need to wash the car.

sections.title: Can I use PPF and ceramic coating together?
sections.text: Yes. PPF goes on prepared paint first, then a compatible ceramic coating can go over the film. You can also coat the exposed paint on panels without PPF. The products need to work together, and both need the right preparation and curing time.

sections.title: Do I need both on the whole car?
sections.text: No. You might choose full-front PPF for the panels most exposed to road debris and ceramic coating for easier cleaning across the car. Full-body PPF is another option if you want more paint covered. Tell us about your driving, the paint condition and your budget so we can quote the combination that fits.

title: Ceramic vs. carbon tint: how to compare the film
description: Compare tint by measured performance, appearance and driving needs instead of assuming the material name answers every question.

sections.title: Is ceramic tint better than carbon tint?
sections.text: Drivers often compare ceramic and carbon films as if one word settles the choice. It does not. Film construction, visible light transmission, solar performance, infrared measurement, UV rejection, glare reduction and warranty all matter. A shade number describes how much visible light passes through a film; it does not by itself describe heat performance. The glass underneath also changes the combined result.

sections.title: What the verified XPEL data shows
sections.text: XPEL's PRIME USA specification sheet lists separate values for VLT, solar energy, IR rejection, UV rejection and glare reduction by variant. The listed XR PLUS variants show 99% UV rejection in that specification, while VLT and infrared values vary by shade. That is the useful comparison habit: ask for the actual product data and compare the variant you are considering. Do not turn one manufacturer's table into a promise for every ceramic or carbon film.

sections.title: Match the choice to your drive
sections.text: If cabin heat and glare are your primary concerns, ask how the proposed film's measured solar and infrared performance fits your glass and use. If appearance, privacy or a particular shade matters most, discuss nighttime visibility and the legal light-transmission requirement together. Existing factory privacy glass can make the final reading and appearance different from the film alone.

sections.title: Does Auto Vos install carbon tint?
sections.text: Auto Vos advertises XPEL PRIME XR Plus ceramic window tint. Carbon tint is not a confirmed part of the current lineup. If you’re comparing quotes, ask for the exact film and shade from each shop, then compare heat rejection, visibility, price and warranty. A darker sample does not automatically mean better heat reduction.

title: Does PPF protect against hail?
description: PPF will not make your car hail-proof. It helps with small stone chips and scuffs, but hail can still dent panels and damage paint.

sections.title: What PPF is designed to do
sections.text: XPEL describes ULTIMATE PLUS as a polyurethane film designed to help protect automotive paint from stone chips and abrasion. Its product page also discusses scratches, rock chips and environmental contaminants, and its technical sheet describes light-scratch healing. That supports a practical conclusion: PPF is useful as a barrier against defined kinds of road wear. It does not support a promise that a vehicle will be hail-proof.

sections.title: Hail is a different impact
sections.text: Hail can dent metal, crack glass and damage film or paint. The size of the hail and the force of the impact affect the damage. PPF is not a substitute for covered parking, and having film does not determine whether an insurance claim is covered.

sections.title: What to do after a storm
sections.text: Photograph the vehicle before attempting repairs, look for dents and film damage, and contact your insurer and a qualified repair or installation professional as appropriate. Do not pick at a lifted edge or polish aggressively over damaged film. A shop can inspect whether the film can remain, needs repair or should be replaced after the underlying panel is evaluated.

sections.title: Should I buy PPF for hail protection?
sections.text: No. Choose PPF if you want help protecting your paint from small road chips and everyday scuffs. For hail, prioritize covered parking when possible. If your car already has storm damage, have the panels inspected before arranging replacement film.
